source_transcript: The Halber steps over whole streets and takes whatever is exactly in the middle, the middle house, the middle seat, the middle child, so we do everything in even numbers. Last night, my brother was born. Now there are three of us. I'm the middle one. My sister, Philippa, is two years older. She still holds my hand on every street. Mom and Dad say, two kids and a baby. I counted three. They write him in the town book tomorrow. I haven't told anyone. Every table here has two chairs or four. We count before we sit. When a street counts one house too many, we build another. Nobody lives there. The church bell skips new. We go from eleven straight to one. The Halber counts houses with houses, kids with kids. When it takes a middle house, there's no gap. By morning, the two neighbors share a wall. Grandma's map puts our two seas a month apart. The middle of her map is blank. No one has ever seen the middle of the world. By breakfast, Philippa told the lady next door. The lady came back with her son. Borrow ours. She said. Then you're four. He sat next to me. He ate all my bread. He called my mom. Mom. At supper, his mother came back for him. Sorry. She said. Without him, we're three. Then my teacher knocked. A baby doesn't count until he walks. She said. Mom said. He's a whole baby. My teacher pinned a note on our door anyway. The note said. He can't walk yet. Then dad packed my bag. You'll sleep at your uncles tonight. He said. I got as far as the doorstep. Mom took the bag out of my hand. On the road, he's alone. She said. A kid alone is his own middle. At sunset, the ground shook twice. Two legs came down at both ends of our street. Our street has four houses. It can't take a house. So what did it come for? It bent down to our kitchen window. One long arm hangs from where its legs meet. It has no face. But it stopped at Philippa. Then me, then the baby. The baby counted. It was counting us. I didn't think. I ran out the front door. I left two kids inside. Two has no middle. The arms stayed at the window. Behind me, Philippa banged on the glass. Then the arm turned. I was alone on the street. I was my own middle. It came after me. Slow and low. I ran up hill to the bus stop. A woman stood there. I stood right next to her. Two. The arms stopped. I saw every house below pressed against the next. And I saw two seas at once. Grandma's map says they're a month apart. It doesn't want the middle. It wants the two sides to meet. Each time it takes a middle, the world gets shorter. No one has ever seen the middle of the world. It took that first. As long as I stayed in a pair, I was safe. Me and this stranger. I asked, can I stand here? As long as you like. She said, the arm hung above us. Then our front door opened. Philippa came running up the hill. Don't stand alone. She yelled. She grabbed my other hand. She was smiling. She thought she'd saved me. The bus came. She let it go. She was staying for me. I counted like we do before we sit. Three. Now the two legs are coming down. One on each side of us. Back in our kitchen. The baby is an only child. One child alone is a middle too. I'm the middle one again.
